articles.excerpt: Short answer: The two tools sit at different layers and compose cleanly. Cursor writes the code and drives the agent; Powerduck defines the contract, generates the typed tools and mock, and verifies r…
articles.body: Short answer: The two tools sit at different layers and compose cleanly. Cursor writes the code and drives the agent; Powerduck defines the contract, generates the typed tools and mock, and verifies responses. Trying to make one replace the other gives up either the editor's speed or the contract's correctness. The division of responsibility Layer Tool What it guarantees Writing code Cursor Fast, context-aware changes Defining the API Powerduck A single, valid contract Agent tools Powerduck generates, Cursor consumes Typed, current tools Development target Powerduck mock Deterministic, contract-shaped Conformance Powerduck Responses match the spec Why the combination is stronger An editor alone is fast but blind to the API; a studio alone is correct but does not write the rest of the code.…

articles.title: Migrating from Manual Cursor API Prompts to Spec-Driven Tools
articles.excerpt: Short answer: Stop paying an agent to re-derive the API from pasted notes. Put the OpenAPI file in the repo, generate the tools and mock from it, and let the agent read the current contract every sess…
articles.body: Short answer: Stop paying an agent to re-derive the API from pasted notes. Put the OpenAPI file in the repo, generate the tools and mock from it, and let the agent read the current contract every session. The migration is incremental: establish the contract, wire the tools, then retire the prompt notes as the agent proves it works. What the manual pattern costs Pasting curl commands and endpoint notes into the chat is a per-session tax. The agent re-reads, re-derives, and re-types the same facts, and any stale note becomes a confident error. The knowledge lives in the conversation, not in a maintained artifact. The migration in stages Establish the contract: convert the existing requests and notes into an OpenAPI file kept in the repo.

articles.title: font-display: swap Fixes Invisible Text. It Also Shifts Your Layout.
articles.excerpt: The ticket said "homepage CLS regressed after the rebrand." Nobody had touched the layout. Nobody had touched the images. The only diff in that deploy was a font swap — the body copy went from a syste…
articles.body: The ticket said "homepage CLS regressed after the rebrand." Nobody had touched the layout. Nobody had touched the images. The only diff in that deploy was a font swap — the body copy went from a system font to a licensed one, loaded from @font-face . Lighthouse didn't care that the new font looked better. It saw text that painted in one spot, then jumped, and it scored that jump like it scores a banner ad shoving the article down the page. The fix everyone reaches for here is font-display: swap . It was already set. That was the problem. The belief: "swap" is the whole fix Here's the belief, and it's not wrong, exactly: web fonts load over the network, and by default most browsers render nothing until the font arrives — the flash of invisible text, FOIT.

articles.title: Local-First API Mocking for Cursor Agents
articles.excerpt: Short answer: Give the agent a local mock generated from the spec, not a live backend. It is deterministic, contract-shaped, and returns the edge cases on demand, with no account and no risk to shared…
articles.body: Short answer: Give the agent a local mock generated from the spec, not a live backend. It is deterministic, contract-shaped, and returns the edge cases on demand, with no account and no risk to shared data. The agent develops against the same contract the tests assert, and the mock regenerates when the spec changes. Why a live backend is the wrong target An agent hitting a real server mutates shared state, hits rate limits, and is slow. Worse, it cannot reproduce the rare failure: the 429, the empty list, the malformed response. The agent optimizes against the happy path because that is all the server reliably offers. What a generated mock provides Determinism: the same request returns the same response, so the agent can iterate.
articles.author: Jeff

articles.title: API Testing in Cursor vs a Contract-Verified Workflow
articles.excerpt: Short answer: An editor can write a test, but it cannot prove the response conforms to the API. A contract-verified workflow checks each response against the schema and flags the field that is silentl…
articles.body: Short answer: An editor can write a test, but it cannot prove the response conforms to the API. A contract-verified workflow checks each response against the schema and flags the field that is silently wrong, so drift is caught at the moment it happens rather than in a flaky test or a staging incident. The tests an editor writes well Cursor is good at generating the happy path: arrange a request, assert a status, check a field. This covers the shape the model expects. The gap is that the test asserts the guess, not the contract, so a response that violates the API can pass if the test never looks at the offending field.
articles.author: Jeff

articles.title: Why Cursor Hallucinates API Calls Without a Spec
articles.excerpt: Short answer: An agent hallucinates an API call because it is predicting the next token, not reading your server. Without a contract, it fills in the endpoint, parameters, and body from patterns and p…
articles.body: Short answer: An agent hallucinates an API call because it is predicting the next token, not reading your server. Without a contract, it fills in the endpoint, parameters, and body from patterns and partial code. The call is the most plausible guess, not knowledge. Giving it a machine-readable contract is the direct fix. Why the guesses are so convincing REST APIs follow conventions. Paths are plural nouns, methods are predictable, and bodies mirror the resource. A model trained on millions of codebases produces a call that fits the convention perfectly, which is why it passes review and fails at runtime. The convention is the camouflage. Where the guesses break Paths: the real endpoint is /v2/orders or uses a verb the model did not expect.
articles.author: Jeff

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 28, 1971: Britain launches its 1st satellite Prospero into space on a Black Arrow rocket
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. The satellite was named Prospero, but it was also known as the X-3. This wasn't Britain's first satellite , but it was the first and only one the British space program launched with one of its own rockets. The first six British satellites all launched from the United States on NASA rockets. Prospero launched on a carrier rocket called the Black Arrow. The Prospero mission was the fourth and final flight of a Black Arrow rocket . Prospero was designed to study how the environment in space affects communications satellites. It tested things solar cells and telemetry systems, and even had a micrometeoroid detector that would determine small particles in space posed a threat to the spacecraft.

articles.title: 5 days beneath the waves: What it's like to live in an underwater 'space station'
articles.excerpt: Confined inside a research station 22 feet (7 meters) underwater, Analog Astronaut Commander Dr. Musilova and her crew performed research and maintenance activities like future astronauts on Mars.
articles.body: Living underwater was surprisingly peaceful. It was in many ways exactly what I imagine living on Mars would be like one day. There were no humans around us, except for my three SEA STAR crewmembers and me. Apart from the human noises we made, we couldn't hear anything other than the life support systems keeping us alive submerged 22 feet (7 meters) below the surface. We were living in these extreme conditions to study the challenges astronauts may face on long-duration space missions. Since performing research in space is still rare and expensive, there are numerous facilities around the world that focus on recreating space-like conditions on Earth . One of those stations is the Jules' Undersea Lab, where the SEA STAR simulated space mission took place.

articles.title: ISS astronaut will conduct Canada's 1st spacewalk in 7 years on Oct. 29: Watch it live
articles.excerpt: Joshua Kutryk will venture outside the International Space Station on Oct. 29, on the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut in more than seven years. Here's how to watch it live.
articles.body: The next International Space Station (ISS) spacewalk will have more maple-leaf flavor than usual, as a Canadian astronaut will become the first to go outside the orbiting complex in seven years. Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, who's also a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force, will help the ISS boost its power supply during his first-ever spacewalk on Thursday (Oct. 29). Kutryk will be joined by NASA astronaut Anil Menon, who has done three spacewalks already and also serves as a colonel with the U.S. Space Force . The duo are scheduled to venture outside the orbiting lab at 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), kicking off a spacewalk that will last roughly 6 hours and 45 minutes. You can watch it live here at Space.com , courtesy of NASA, beginning at 6:30 a.m. EDT (1030 GMT).

articles.title: Meet Apeiron, Virgin Galactic's 1st 'Delta-class' space plane
articles.excerpt: Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled its first "Delta-class" space plane, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name.
articles.body: Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled the first space plane in its next-gen "Delta" line, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name. Spaceship Apeiron will be the first Delta-class vehicle, Virgin Galactic revealed on Wednesday (Oct. 28). Apeiron (pronounced "A'-per-on," according to the announcement) takes its name from the ancient Greek word meaning "boundless," and was selected through a public poll that drew votes from thousands of people across 83 countries and six continents. The reveal comes on the same day that the space plane is scheduled to be flown from its manufacturing facility in Mesa, Arizona, to Spaceport America in New Mexico, where the vehicle will undergo final preparations before beginning flight tests.

articles.title: China's secretive space plane caught on camera in incredible new photo released by US military
articles.excerpt: A U.S. military intelligence agency has released an incredible new photograph of China's secretive space plane, showing it docked to another spacecraft in orbit.
articles.body: A photograph of China's reusable Shenlong space plane docked to another spacecraft, taken by Vantor's WorldView 3 satellite from a distance of 56 miles (90 kilometers). (Image credit: Satellite image ©2026 Vantor) A U.S. military intelligence agency has released an incredible new photograph of China's secretive space plane, showing it docked to another spacecraft in orbit. The photograph was taken in 2024 by Vantor's WorldView 3 satellite, from a distance of 56 miles (90 kilometers). Ground-based observers have previously photographed Shenlong in orbit , but this new photo from Vantor, taken from space, reveals new details about the mysterious spacecraft in stunning clarity, with a resolution of 4.5 centimeters (1.8 inches) per pixel.

articles.title: The final ‘Dune: Part Three’ trailer reignites war on Arrakis and leaves us with more questions than answers
articles.excerpt: The spoilerific final look at Denis Villeneuve's third and final sci-fi epic is loaded with action and drama that set it apart from Dune: Messiah's pages.
articles.body: Dune: Part Three 's marketing campaign has been a long and generous one, but Warner Bros. and Legendary Pictures knew an extra push was needed in order to compete with Avengers: Doomsday , as both sci-fi blockbusters will be releasing next to each other at Christmas. In its final trailer, Denis Villeneuve's threequel goes all out. This isn't the first time a Dune: Part Three trailer has left us with more questions than answers , but the in-depth look at the character dynamics and plot beats that await will make longtime fans of Frank Herbert's works raise their eyebrows. Messiah, the second installment in the book series, is a novel of long monologues and very tense conversations.
